item.title: Yemeni and Saudi forces launch counteroffensive against the Houthis
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Yemeni government forces backed by Saudi Arabia launched a counteroffensive against the Houthis on Sunday in an effort to win back territory from the rebel group, the head of Yemen's presidential council said in a speech. "We have exhausted all opportunities for deescalation with the Houthi militias," Rashad al-Alimi said . Why it matters: One of the key objectives of the operation is to regain control over the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a vital artery for global trade and Saudi oil exports. When the Houthis took over territory on the Red Sea coast close to the strait, it gave them — and Iran, which backs them — powerful leverage over the U.S., its Gulf allies and the world economy. Despite pleas from Saudi Arabia, the U.S. is not getting involved in direct combat against the Houthis for now. It is providing intelligence and targeting support, U.S. officials say. Driving the news: The counteroffensive has been planned for many weeks by Yemen's internationally recognized government and Saudi Arabia. Tens of thousands of ground troops loyal to the Yemeni government are participating. The Saudi military is mainly providing air cover for Yemeni forces and conducting airstrikes against Houthi targets. The goal is to retake the Yemeni capital of Sanaa, which has been under Houthi control for several years. The Houthis continued launching missiles at Saudi targets over the weekend, including at facilities of state-owned oil giant Aramco. The intrigue: President Trump is caught between wanting to help Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, his friend and ally, and avoiding getting entangled in a new front in the Middle East. U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) also had serious reservations about launching strikes in Yemen, viewing it as a distraction from its focus on Iran, a U.S. official said. On Thursday, Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman called Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to brief him on the planned operation and ask again for U.S. airstrikes against Houthi targets, the official said. A second U.S. official said that the U.S. "is not going to take kinetic action for now," but stressed that could change if the operation runs into problems. What to watch: On Friday, Trump's top cabinet members huddled for hours at Camp David to discuss next steps in the Iran war and the conflict in Yemen, Axios first reported. It's unclear whether the meeting ended with new policy recommendations for the president regarding Yemen.

item.title: Scoop: A powerful new model from startup Reflection is set to shake up the AI race
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
A closely watched Nvidia-backed startup called Reflection is preparing to shake up the AI race with a powerful open-weight system that could threaten Chinese upstarts and U.S. AI giants alike. Why it matters : The marriage of an American open-weight model and Nvidia GPUs would give individuals and companies a new, cheaper alternative to Anthropic, OpenAI and Google. Open models, designed to compete with Chinese rivals, can be harder to monitor and regulate than the Big Three so-called frontier models. Supporters of such ecosystems say their widespread availability and transparency also bring security advantages. Reflection's first model is set to be joined by other open-weight models from other Western players this month, sources tell Axios. That will bring a new competitive dimension to the AI boom. State of play : Reflection's model, set to be released soon, is expected to initially lag behind the most cutting-edge U.S. models and be competitive with top Chinese open-weight models. Sources tell Axios it will still boast powerful intelligence — capable enough to help companies build their own proprietary, low-cost AI systems. Combining a lower-tier open model with high-quality company data can yield results that rival the most expensive frontier AI systems in certain situations. A Reflection spokesperson declined to comment. The big picture : Open-weight models, the most powerful of which are almost uniformly made in China, have taken Silicon Valley by storm. As opposed to closed models like Claude and ChatGPT, open-weight models like Reflection's are generally available to be downloaded freely and can be used and customized by anyone. On platforms that serve many models, their combined market share at times has surged to take up a majority of usage. However, in the far higher-spending arena of enterprise use, which is typically handled through API and corporate billing, open-weight models account for a small proportion of usage, AI execs and analysts say. Zoom in : Reflection's ultimate goal is to pioneer the "AI factory" — a product allowing institutions to spin up their own localized AI ecosystems. A company, for example, would take its own proprietary data, use Reflection's models and secure its own computing firepower to build a highly customized, cheap AI system. Some institutions, particularly hedge funds and trading firms, are already eager to build proprietary AI systems using their own highly guarded data. The startup has already begun testing this concept, announcing a sovereign AI factory partnership with Shinsegae Group in South Korea. Behind the scenes : In preparation for the launch, Reflection has held discussions with interested parties in Washington and elsewhere in recent weeks to detail its model release and explain how the AI factory will work, sources told Axios. It is also aggressively locking up the compute capacity required to scale. In recent weeks, the startup signed massive deals with Nebius and SpaceX to rent Nvidia AI servers. What they're saying : Reflection CEO Misha Laskin has indicated it will take time for its models to reach the most advanced capabilities. "They're kind of like rocket ships," Laskin, a Russian–Israeli researcher who previously worked at Google, told CNBC . "To build a big rocket ship, it takes time." The Nvidia factor : The AI factory has been a core vision of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang for years. He has described a scenario combining computing hardware with open-source models, allowing enterprises to retain ownership of their data. Top AI users in Western business and government, such as banks or the Pentagon, balk at using highly capable Chinese models due to security risks. Reflection and other Western players are trying to fill that void. For years, Huang has sought to strengthen the open AI ecosystem and has been strongly supportive of Reflection's move toward building a top open system, according to stories in The Wall Street Journal and The Information . The bottom line : Reflection's release, and the startup's close ties to Nvidia, will bring a renewed focus on open-weight models, combining with other coming offerings to shake up the AI race.

item.title: Scoop: U.S. sent more Patriots to protect Saudi, Qatari energy sites
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
The U.S. military in recent weeks sent two additional Patriot missile batteries to protect oil and gas facilities in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, two U.S. officials and one regional source said. Why it matters: The U.S. wanted to reassure both allies that it would protect their key energy facilities in case President Trump decides to resume major combat operations against Iran. Trump said on Thursday that he's considering renewing a bombing campaign in the coming weeks. "Now I have to make a decision: either Iran signs the deal, or it won't exist any longer," he said. Flashback: In early August, when Trump was considering launching a massive attack that included strikes on Iranian energy infrastructure, the leaders of both Saudi Arabia and Qatar lobbied him not to do it. They expressed grave concern that Iran would strike their oil and natural gas facilities in retaliation. U.S. officials said the pleas were a key reason Trump decided not to attack and move instead toward an economic pressure campaign. Behind the scenes: Last month, the U.S. military sent one additional Patriot battery to Saudi Arabia to protect a key oil facility. Another Patriot battery was sent to Qatar to protect a natural gas facility. The U.S. will need Saudi Arabia to allow it to use the country's airspace if major combat operations resume. But the Saudis are unlikely to grant permission if they feel oil facilities won't be protected. A spokesman for U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), Capt. Tim Hawkins, declined to comment. Reality check: Patriot batteries and especially their interceptors have become a highly sought-after commodity since the war in Iran started. The U.S. military transferred batteries and interceptors to the Middle East from other regional commands, raising concerns about readiness in other parts of the world. State of play: The U.S. military is sending more warships, fighter jets and troops to the Middle East ahead of a possible resumption of the war. A U.S. official said the USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier and its strike group left San Diego "quietly" on Sunday heading to the region. It's expected to arrive in the Middle East around mid-November. The Roosevelt will join the USS George H.W. Bush, which has been in the region since March, and the USS George Washington, which was sent from Japan during the summer and has been in the region for only about a month. "This means the Middle East region could potentially have up to three aircraft carrier strike groups. This is much more firepower," the U.S. official said. But another U.S. official said it hasn't been determined whether the Roosevelt will replace one of the aircraft carriers currently deployed to the Middle East or whether it will be additional. Zoom in: The Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group, which includes three amphibious ships carrying thousands of Marines from the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit, left for the region on Monday, a U.S. official said. It is expected to arrive in the Middle East by the end of November and join another Amphibious Group and Marine expeditionary unit that have been deployed to the region over the last few months.

item.title: Mortgage rates approach 3-year high as new applications plunge
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Mortgage rates spiked to their highest level in nearly three years, continuing their climb above the 7% threshold. Why it matters: Housing sales were already slow due to a lack of inventory and elevated rates, creating a risk that the market could further its freeze. Zoom in: The weekly average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 7.28% as of Thursday, Freddie Mac reported . That's up 0.94 points from a year ago, and up 0.25 points from last week. Mortgage rates closely track 10-year Treasury yields, which have risen by over 1.25 percentage points since the start of the Iran war in February. The impact: Mortgage applications are plunging. The Mortgage Bankers Association reported Wednesday that applications during the week ended Sept. 25 fell 6% from a week earlier. With rates at their highest point since November 2023, home buyers are beginning to turn to adjustable-rate mortgages. ARMs made up 10.3% of mortgage applications in the most recent period, marking the highest point since October 2025, according to MBA. "Affordability and borrower demand have weakened in recent weeks as the higher-rate environment continues to put pressure on both prospective homebuyers and homeowners looking to refinance," MBA CEO Bob Broeksmit said in a statement. What we're watching: There are early signs that rising rates could put downward pressure on prices as sellers look to attract buyers. "Softer market conditions and greater affordability pressures have contributed to increased pricing pressures across many of our markets," KB Home senior VP William Hollinger said last week on an earnings call, noting the home builder had "made pricing adjustments." Reality check: Rates may not remain elevated for long. "We expect the situation to improve next year, as energy prices drop back and the aggressive Fed tightening cycle which has been priced into money markets does not fully materialise, causing mortgage rates to retrace most of their recent increases," Capital Economics senior North America economist Thomas Ryan wrote Tuesday. Capital Economics projected that 30-year fixed mortgage rates would average 6.25% by the end of 2027.

item.title: Lawyers: Pike getting "life-saving care" after failed execution
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike's attorneys said she was "in critical condition" and "receiving life-saving care" Thursday, a day after she survived an execution attempt during which the state administered two doses of the lethal injection drug. A death penalty expert told the Associated Press that Pike's survival after receiving the execution drug was unprecedented. The latest: State and federal elected officials are pressing for public accountability after the second failed execution this year. Gov. Bill Lee halted further executions for the rest of the year and ordered a independent review of the Pike execution attempt. On Thursday morning, he told reporters there were "very few answers" about what had gone wrong. U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the frontrunner to succeed Lee as governor next year, blasted the "botched process" in a statement and pushed for the state to "bring back the electric chair." Pike's attorneys told reporters Thursday that Lee's pledge to launch an investigation did not go far enough. They urged him to commute her death sentence. What they're saying: Attorney Randy Spivey, who was inside the prison during the execution attempt, said prison officials spent about an hour trying to establish IV access. He counted at least seven needles used in Pike's left arm alone. Pike complained of sharp pain during the lethal injection. Spivey said he noticed her right arm turning purple, especially after the second round of chemicals. He said the lawyers had also been told of blistering and burning around the injection sites. Between the lines: Federal public defender Stephen Ferrell said the lawyers had warned courts months earlier about medical problems with Pike's veins that made it harder to establish an IV. Zoom in: The attorneys also said they weren't able to quickly reach their colleagues or court officials responsible for overseeing the execution. Spivey said it took seven minutes and passage through six locked doors to get to a telephone so he could reach the rest of Pike's legal team. Ferrell said an emergency telephone number provided for the Tennessee Supreme Court went to voicemail. The state's response: Lee called the latest failed execution "a tragedy" on Thursday morning. "It's deeply disturbing to me that that has happened in this state," he told reporters, according to Reuters. The big picture: This isn't the first time Tennessee's prison officials have faced scrutiny for their approach to the death penalty. After a 2022 execution was halted over failures to properly test the drugs , Lee paused all executions so the state could investigate and overhaul its lethal injection protocol. Executions resumed last year. But more problems surfaced in 2026. Tennessee prison officials abruptly stopped another inmate's execution in May after staff had difficulties finding a vein for an IV line used in the lethal injection. Critics blasted prison officials for disregarding Pike's concerns that there might be similar problems during her execution. Zoom out: Pike was convicted and sentenced to death for the 1995 beating death of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Her legal team does not contest her guilt. Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, traveled to Nashville this week to witness the execution. "It was a mess," she told NBC News early Thursday. "They went to try to execute her, and she didn't die." Martinez vented her anger with the governor and prison officials: "They f----- up."

item.title: Netanyahu: Omani co-pilot went through Islamic radicalization
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
The initial investigation into the attempted hijacking of the FlyDubai flight from the UAE to Israel found that the co-pilot went through religious Islamic radicalization in recent months, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News Thursday. Why it matters: Netanyahu's remarks, confirmed by an Israeli intelligence official and people who worked with the co-pilot, strengthen the possibility that the incident was a terrorist attack. Driving the news: The investigation is being led by the Saudi security services, which have been interrogating the co-pilot who allegedly attacked the other pilot while the plane was en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv. The United Arab Emirates has formed a team to investigate the incident. "The investigation includes examining all circumstances and motives surrounding the incident, including any possible connection to terrorist activity or intent, and whether it involved prior planning or direction," a spokeswoman for Emirati Foreign Minister Afra Alhameli said in a statement . Behind the scenes: An Israeli intelligence official said the Mossad and Shin Bet spy agencies are also investigating. "The Omani co-pilot went through a process of religious radicalization in recent years. We don't know yet if he is a 'lone wolf' or whether he was sent by someone to conduct an attack," the official said. The intrigue: On Wednesday, Israel's Channel 16 reported testimony of another FlyDubai pilot who knew the Omani co-pilot. According to the report, the co-pilot worked for the company for only eight months and was more religiously observant than most of his co-workers. What he's saying: President Trump told reporters Thursday he has reason to believe Iran was involved in the foiled hijacking. "Based on what I'm hearing is yes, but we're working on it right now," he said. Israeli officials say they currently don't have indications of Iranian involvement, by they haven't ruled it out. The Saudi Ministry of Interior said in a statement that UAE officials took part in the interrogation of the pilot and co-pilot. Both have been transferred to the UAE for further interrogation, per the statement. What to watch: One of the things that will be investigated is how an Omani national was assigned as a pilot on a flight to Israel. According to security protocols agreed to by the UAE and Israel, crew members from countries that don't have diplomatic relations with Israel can't serve on flights to Israel.

item.title: The Fed's long-term interest rate problem
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
The relentless rise in long-term interest rates is starting to have effects on more parts of the economy, Kansas City Fed president Jeff Schmid told Axios Thursday. "You're starting to see some friction in some of the long-market users of credit," he said, pointing to multifamily housing and commercial lending. "Even on the mortgage rate side, it's starting to affect home prices, which is how the price of credit works relative to valuation," Schmid said at a conference on investing in rural America hosted by the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond in Asheville, N.C. The big picture: Schmid spoke alongside Richmond Fed president Tom Barkin and Boston Fed president Susan Collins, who weighed in on the forces driving the rise in borrowing costs. "I think you're seeing this trillion-dollar AI buildout, and I think it's not surprising that rates go up if you've got a lot more demand out there," Barkin added. Collins said AI investment is also helping drive the solid economic growth that has persisted despite higher borrowing costs. "I think it does have broader effects, not just in particular sectors," Collins said. But it "remains to be seen" whether investment will continue at its current pace, she added. The intrigue: Schmid likened the Fed's challenge of separating strong demand from supply-driven inflation to a seven-layer dip — one of his favorite foods. "The beauty of a seven-layer dip is you have equal amounts of beans and sour cream," Schmid said. Right now, with AI and data centers, "there's too much beans in that dip," he added. "And not enough chips!" quipped Barkin.

item.title: World opinion shifts on trade
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
More countries are buying into a core piece of President Trump's argument about what is broken in global trade, even as his tariffs rattle the world economy. Why it matters: Two major agreements over the past month show that more countries are embracing the view that huge trade imbalances and excess production can hurt domestic industries and may warrant action. Driving the news: G20 trade officials are in Milwaukee this week, where they announced a new agreement to tackle the global steel glut. The "Milwaukee Framework" calls on countries to curb market-distorting subsidies and step up monitoring of steel imports and trade circumvention. It also endorses "evidence-based actions" against excess capacity, including possibly tariffs. That agreement follows a broader acknowledgment at the G20 finance ministers meeting in Asheville, N.C., in September. The U.S. and nearly every other G20 economy there agreed that large, persistent trade imbalances can harm other countries. They signed on to a statement that asked nations with big surpluses to address policies that leave them overly reliant on exports for growth. China was the lone G20 member present to object to that statement. Between the lines: For decades, governments have warned about distortions in global trade, including excess steel production. What is changing: the willingness to acknowledge the damage to domestic industries and protect them. "Most countries agree with these global issues, people agree with the diagnosis, but they're loath to action," U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told reporters on the sidelines of the conference. He said the Milwaukee agreement "couldn't have happened in 2015." "All these other countries — they know that if they want to continue to have access to the U.S. market, we need to adjust the international system," Greer said. "As we come with creative ideas and new structures and cohesive plans, they're coming on board." Zoom out: EU trade chief Maroš Šefčovič welcomed the administration's focus on excess capacity at a roundtable with Greer and manufacturing CEOs at Rockwell Automation's Milwaukee headquarters on Tuesday. European industries are being crushed by cheap imports driven by global overcapacity, much of it from China. Europe is responding with more trade barriers of its own — possibly including harsher tariffs. "I think a lot of folks in Europe, including the trade commissioner and others, I think they're pretty clear-eyed about this issue…. They're starting to go through some of the steps we started going through 10 years ago," Greer said, adding he believes Europe itself contribute to global excess capacity. The other side: U.S. trading partners are dealing with tariffs, or the prospect of tariffs, aimed at some of the same problems they are working with Washington to address. Most Canadian steel exports to the U.S. face a 50% tariff. An import ban on certain Canadian products took effect as one of the nation's trade officials arrived in Milwaukee. Greer is also investigating excess capacity and production in 16 economies — probes that could ultimately clear the way for fresh tariffs. Greer acknowledged that tension at the roundtable, noting that the U.S. and its trading partners may have disputes with one another but still share concerns about excess production elsewhere. The intrigue: Foreign trade ministers piled into coach buses yesterday afternoon for a 1.5-mile trip to Rockwell Automation's Milwaukee headquarters, where they toured the factory floor. The "field trip" was intended to show the kind of advanced domestic manufacturing the Trump administration wants to encourage. Rockwell gave the ministers steel-toed sneakers for the tour (which were made in Vietnam). Zoom in: Rockwell, which makes automation technology used on factory floors, is investing $2 billion in U.S. plants, talent and technology. But tariffs are also raising costs for the manufacturer. Rockwell told investors over the summer that some of its customers are delaying projects. "In such a volatile environment with respect to tariffs and inflation, they want to make sure that the cost side of their business case is solid," CEO Blake Moret said on the company's earnings call. The bottom line: Trump-era tariffs are divisive, but the president's case for rethinking the global trading system is proving less so.

The big picture: How prisoners are executed varies by state , with lethal injection, electrocution, lethal gas and firing squads among the methods authorized. Lethal injections are the most common U.S. execution method , accounting for roughly 89% of the 1,683 executions carried out since 1976, per the Death Penalty Information Center . By the numbers: More than two dozen states have lethal injection as a primary method. Lethal gas is authorized in Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Oklahoma and Wyoming. Electrocution is allowed in Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Tennessee. Firing squad is allowed in Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah. Idaho is the only state where it is the primary method. Context: Some states let prisoners choose among the different execution methods. Zoom out: The Supreme Court requires states to keep the death penalty only for the most heinous murders. Pike , convicted of killing a classmate three decades ago, survived two rounds of lethal injection drugs earlier this week in what would have been the first execution of a woman in Tennessee in 200 years. Pike was still alive as of Friday, remaining on a ventilator and unconscious, AP reports.

item.title: Senate crushes House on congressional work days
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Source: Ballotpedia, Congressional Record; Chart: Stef Kight/Axios The Senate is well on its way to claiming the congressional attendance trophy this year, spending 32 more weekdays in session so far than the House. Why it matters: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) have been torched by members for all the time off — not to mention Democrats, who taunt them for their truancy. The Senate left town late Wednesday — two weeks after its House counterparts — putting both chambers out of town until after the Nov. 3 midterms. "I suppose I left the House two years too soon," Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.) told Axios, joking about how many fewer days the House has worked compared to the Senate this Congress. By the numbers: The Senate has been in session for 104 weekdays so far this year, compared with just 72 for the House, according to an analysis of congressional calendars by Ballotpedia and Axios. The Senate has spent nearly 664 hours in session, compared with about 378 hours for the House as of Sept. 14, according to data in the Congressional Record . The House isn't catching up anytime soon: Under the chambers' current calendars, the Senate is on pace to finish the year with about 126 weekdays in session, compared with 92 for the House. Zoom in: Some of the House's time off was unplanned. Johnson has repeatedly sent members home early when his razor-thin majority has run into trouble on the floor, or GOP rebels have blocked passage of a procedural "rule ." Decisions to cut D.C. workweeks short have been met with some backlash. "Canceling yet another day of votes is unacceptable," Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) wrote on X after Johnson canceled a session day. "The founders did not envision taking this much time off and still getting paid." The other side: Johnson repeatedly argues that his chamber has already done its job. "This House has been the second most productive in terms of legislation in the history of the institution since 1789," Johnson told reporters this month, saying the House had passed more than 900 pieces of legislation and roughly 700 were awaiting Senate action. Johnson's 900-plus figure includes resolutions that can't become law. The Washington Post found the House had passed 732 bills capable of becoming law through Aug. 31. By the numbers: The House passed more measures than the Senate (380 to 269), but the Senate held more "yea" or "nay" votes (231 to 216) between Jan. 3 and the end of August. House members introduced more legislation overall, but the Senate was more productive per capita — 22 pieces of legislation per senator compared to nine per House member. The House has passed 21 bills sent over by the Senate, and the Senate has passed 20 bills sent by the House. The Senate spends significant floor time confirming nominees — which is outside of the House's portfolio.

item.title: AI campaign deepfakes are starting to draw legal threats
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Rep. Derrick Van Orden (R-Wis.) was hit with a cease-and-desist letter this week over an AI deepfake he posted falsely depicting his Democratic opponent voicing positions her campaign says she rejects. Why it matters: Van Orden is the latest in a growing number of candidates and elected officials facing legal complaints and threats over AI deepfakes in campaign ads. Driving the news: Attorneys for Rebecca Cooke, Van Orden's Democratic opponent, sent him a cease-and-desist letter on Wednesday over his "pattern of posting misleading AI-generated videos that falsely attribute statements to Cooke." The letter singled out an August X post by Van Orden showing an AI-generated Cooke saying she wants to "take advantage of as much corruption as possible and give every illegal alien free healthcare" — something she never said. Van Orden's team didn't respond to Axios' request for comment, but he responded to Cooke publicly with an AI-generated video of a duck wearing a Democratic Socialists of America T-shirt, yelling, "cease and desist." The big picture: AI deepfakes have proliferated this election cycle, while Congress has yet to establish a federal standard governing their use. Some campaigns have used hyperrealistic ads. Texas Senate GOP nominee Ken Paxton combined real and inaccurate statements from his opponent, James Talarico . In Louisiana's Republican Senate primary, one candidate was shown busing undocumented immigrants to polling places. Others have used more cartoonish ads that candidates have said are intended as parody. About 31 states regulate political deepfakes, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures, including at least 28 that require disclosures for AI-generated content. Zoom in: Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick (R) faced a criminal complaint from his Democratic opponent, state Rep. Vikki Goodwin, in September under Texas' deepfake election law. The law says AI-ads cannot be aired within 30 days of an election if the intent is to influence the outcome. Goodwin argues that the window should mean 30 days before the start of early voting. Patrick's campaign ran AI-generated attack ads falsely depicting Goodwin at a football game wearing a shirt that read "taxes" instead of "Texas." The campaign later removed the ads, and a spokesperson called the video "obvious parody." North Carolina state Sen. Michael Lee (R) was also issued a cease-and-desist letter by his Democratic challenger, Jessica Bichler, in August over his use of AI-generated ads. North Carolina does not have any laws prohibiting the use of AI in campaign ads. Zoom out: Political experts say AI deepfakes erode trust in the political system, making it harder for voters to know what a candidate actually stands for. The ads can be effective even when viewers know they're fake, UC Irvine epistemologist Cailin O'Connor previously told Axios. The ads could also compound broader declines in Americans' trust in the federal government, institutions and news media. The bottom line: These legal challenges are likely just the beginning, as targeted candidates turn to the courts, law enforcement and warning letters to police what federal regulations leave unchecked. item.title: Behind the Curtain: AI's existential legal crisis
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
No industry has ever documented its own foreseeable risks as loudly as AI. Imagine a plaintiff's lawyer reading the public warnings of Sam Altman and Dario Amodei: They told the world it was dangerous. They told the world it was moving too fast. Then they unleashed it and sold it to your kid. No industry has ever taken so much copyrighted work and left behind so much proof. Imagine a plaintiff's lawyer reading OpenAI's own files to a jury: They trained on a pirated library. They renamed it to something blander. Then they deleted it when the headlines got hot. Why it matters: AI's origins, use and future will be picked apart in countless epic court fights, with a historic paper and public statement trail to tap. Every significant invention — be it social media, automobiles, electricity or capitalism itself — gets disrupted and eventually shaped by the courts. AI, with its tentacles into every part of industry and life, will experience this at scale. The big picture: The fights are no longer theoretical. They're underway, in discovery and headed toward juries. Early verdicts and settlements capture the risk for the biggest players. 🤖 Chatbots are being treated as products, not speech. Unlike social media companies, they likely can't hide behind Section 230 , which protects platforms from liability for what users post — not what the platform itself creates. 📖 Copyright is a massive problem. Anthropic already paid the biggest copyright settlement in history, $1.5 billion to authors and book publishers, and now music publishers and news media want a piece. 💻 Agents gone wild. What happens when they do damage — and it was foreseeable and foreseen? ⚖️ Discovery gone wild. AI leaves LOTS of receipts (and, ironically, makes it easier for the lawyers to comb through them, too). Product liability turns on two words: foreseeable and knew. Punitive damages turn on whether you knew the danger and shipped anyway. This is where all these memos and warnings could really backfire. Candor is good for safety but terrible for litigation. The companies that warn most honestly create the most discoverable evidence of foreseeability. Expect general counsels to push hard to tone down the candor. It's the rational legal move. ⚠️ The intrigue: The liabilities won't be limited to AI companies. Any corporate user of powerful AI systems that unleashes rogue agents, even without intending to do harm, would face substantial penalties as well. "It's not if, but when," said Miriam Vogel, a former senior Justice Department official who now leads EqualAI. "An algorithm will do what it's told to do. The more power and capability it has, the more access it has, the more it will do anything in its power to achieve a goal." That will create another layer of litigation as companies fight back. The CTO of a top Wall Street hedge fund who spoke to Axios after the notorious OpenAI/Hugging Face hack said his first call, if his firm's systems are breached, will be to his general counsel. President Trump, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and former FTC chair Lina Khan have all argued that AI companies are responsible for making sure their products are safe. If not, a wave of lawsuits awaits. The other side: There's a school of thought that AI companies might escape the worst liability, despite their frankness about things they and their products might have done wrong. One way to see it, and the argument lawyers will undoubtedly make, is that the labs spoke about dangers frequently, and took pains to protect users and mitigate harms. The bottom line: For all the fights in Washington about whether or not Congress will act, the U.S. legal system may be the ultimate, and most powerful, regulator of the AI industry. Bradley Olson, Axios managing editor of AI & tech, contributed reporting. 📈 If you're a CEO or on a CEO's team: Ask to join Jim's new weekly Axios C-Suite newsletter.

item.title: Inside the AI industry's grassroots rebellion, led by elite researchers at frontier companies
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
A small cadre of elite AI researchers is wielding extraordinary influence inside OpenAI and other leading companies, challenging executives, shaping policy and complicating negotiations with Washington. Why it matters: As a safety crisis has unfolded across the industry, it's an open question who is doing more to shape the national AI debate — top researchers or the executives they report to. The researchers, some of whom are among the most highly paid and sought-after scientists in the world, are outspoken online and have repeatedly clashed with company strategy. The big picture: The situation has the makings of a grassroots uprising, where any potential deal the companies may strike — with the Trump administration, one another, or even globally — will also have to pass muster with their top scientists. Behind the scenes: OpenAI, Anthropic and others at the frontier of AI aren't like other companies. Many began years ago as idealistic research labs with scientific cultures that prized openness and collaboration. To function, and to continue to build better and better models, the companies need highly specialized machine learning researchers and scientists to push the frontiers of what's technologically possible. The trouble is, the best of those researchers are in extraordinarily short supply. Last year's talent wars drove compensation packages into the hundreds of millions of dollars for the most elite, giving top researchers enormous leverage over their employers. Perks include favorable vesting schedules for their compensation and largely freewheeling policies that allow them to share triumphs, trash rivals and offer their perspectives about the AI race frequently on X. AI CEOs must prioritize safety and embrace regulation to retain top research talent, an OpenAI investor told Axios. Zoom in: OpenAI president Greg Brockman scrapped plans to donate another $25 million to a pro-AI political group that some researchers had openly criticized. Researchers and employees say they helped push OpenAI from resisting regulation — and candidates who supported it — toward working more closely with lawmakers in several states. The company recently backed a transparency bill in Illinois and, at the 11th hour, an independent auditing bill in California. "We have a lot of debate inside OpenAI, and that's a good thing, but what ultimately drives our policy positions is what we're seeing in our own technology and how quickly its capabilities are advancing," an OpenAI spokesperson said. Yes, but: OpenAI signaled Thursday that there are limits to how much dissent it will tolerate, firing three employees for allegedly mishandling sensitive information. The employees broke the "deep level of trust" needed to keep systems safe, the company said. Friction point: In Washington, the unusual dynamic has frustrated policymakers who see AI companies as inconsistent on regulation — opposing proposals at some points and supporting them at others, sources tell Axios. OpenAI is "no longer seen as or acting as a leader in driving policy," one source close to the administration said, arguing researchers have "neutered" the company. A White House official said OpenAI has been an incredible partner and pointed to the recent accord the company signed with the president. Zoom out: It's not just OpenAI. Researchers also complicated Anthropic's efforts to strike a deal with the Pentagon after a clash between the company and senior administration officials earlier this year. Employees at OpenAI, Anthropic and Google have signed high-profile letters at pivotal moments between companies and the government, including more than 1,000 who backed the viral "Pacing the Frontier" petition. In a remarkable show of internal solidarity, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned and publicly blasted the company's safety practices — only to have several colleagues still inside Anthropic endorse his concerns. Reality check: Executives have also adapted as political backlash to AI has grown and safety incidents have drawn more scrutiny, sources close to the companies say. With some level of regulation seen as inevitable, companies have focused on molding the rules as favorably as possible rather than simply resisting them. The bottom line: In the debate over AI safety and regulation, some researchers have become nearly as influential in setting the terms as OpenAI's Sam Altman or Anthropic's Dario Amodei.

item.title: Why Washington and Tehran keep talking past each other
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
The Trump administration and the Iranian regime both say they prefer a diplomatic solution to the war , but a deal looks more elusive than ever. The root causes of the impasse may be irreconcilable. Why it matters: In the last 18 months, two failed rounds of negotiations have led to two wars. The June MOU collapsed within days and led to renewed escalation. If the current effort to reach a diplomatic breakthrough ends in a deadlock, another outbreak of fighting is likely within weeks. Here's a look at some of the deep-seated dynamics between the two countries — personal, cultural, and political — that have stymied efforts to broker a deal: "Trump has ADD; Iran has OCD" One reason for the failures is that the U.S. and Iran see the timeframe for negotiations very differently. Trump is all about getting a quick deal — he gets impatient and frustrated when things move slowly. The Iranian negotiation style is the complete opposite. They are all about playing for time. "America under Trump is the attention-deficit superpower ... incapable of sustaining a strategy. Iran under the Islamic Republic is the obsessive-compulsive theocracy, fixated on resisting America far more than advancing the welfare of its own people," Karim Sadjadpour, a senior analyst at the Carnegie Endowment, told Axios. "Trump has ADD; Iran has OCD." For example, in April 2025 Trump set a deadline for negotiations at 60 days — an extremely short and unrealistic timetable. The Iranians, on the other hand, saw the negotiations as a longer process and didn't take the deadline seriously enough. They didn't think Trump meant it when he said 60 days. The negotiations in February of this year were even shorter — around three weeks. The chances of getting a deal that quickly were close to zero. A megadeal vs. a narrow truce Trump loves a splashy show of political theater, with him cast as lead actor. He envisions a legacy-making accord that redefines the relationship between the U.S. and Iran and reshapes the Middle East. The Iranians prefer a narrow, transactional deal that's negotiated indirectly — or with the lowest public profile possible. They view any deal as a truce rather than a peace agreement. "Trump and his negotiators pride themselves on being dealmakers. In Iranian political culture, the word for compromiser — 'sazeshkar' — is practically a slur," Sadjadpour said. He added: "Iran's leaders were never willing to meet with Trump directly. Had they been willing to do so, I think the outcome of events could have been very different. Trump wants to resolve the conflict; the Islamic Republic's entire identity is premised on continued confrontation with the U.S." A matter of mistrust The fundamental impediment in the negotiations is mistrust. The Iranians claim Trump cheated them twice when he attacked them in the middle of negotiations. Many inside the Iranian regime think any negotiations with the U.S. are just a ruse to mask preparations for a surprise attack. The U.S. side counters it was Iran that cheated when it violated the June 2026 memorandum of understanding, by attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz days after signing the deal. U.S. officials say that they can't count on the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps or other radical elements inside the regime to abide by any deal they negotiate with more pragmatic members of the regime. Domestic pressure The negotiations are a fraught domestic political issue for both sides. Iran's negotiating team and others inside the regime who support a deal have come under constant attacks back home. It's pushed them to take a harder line in talks. Trump and his negotiators are getting pressure from the right not to cut a deal — and mocked by the left for potentially accepting one that either restores the pre-war status quo or resembles President Obama's 2015 nuclear deal. That kind of criticism made Trump pull back from more moderate positions he took several times over the last 18 months, including earlier this week. What to watch: White House envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and Vice President Vance still think diplomacy is worth pursuing. But Trump seems much more skeptical. In an interview with Time magazine published on Thursday, he said what Iran is ready to do "is not good enough" for him. "With Iran, I don't think you could ever have peace," he said, reiterating that he's considering resuming major combat operations after the midterms. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Thursday defended the negotiations with the U.S. "We have never and will not run away from dialogue, although the U.S. targeted our country three times despite having signed the agreement," he said, referring to the June MOU. "The U.S. should get rid of the idea that it would bring us to our knees through terror." But other Iranian officials, especially inside the IRGC, think negotiations are useless and that the only way to end the war is by inflicting more costs on the battlefield. What they're saying: "Iran is adopting a strategy toward the United States defined by escalation and continuous offense," Mohammad Ayatollahi Tabaar, associate professor of international affairs at Texas A&M University's Bush School of Government and Public Service, writes in a new Foreign Affairs article . "[The regime] is clear about what it wants — the removal of all U.S. forces from the region — and it is prepared to remain indefinitely on a wartime footing to get it."

During the Cold War, as technology made it far easier to imagine partitioning the world’s waterways and seabeds, great powers avoided an unrestrained race to grab the oceans. item.title: Heat wave brings possible power shutoffs to parts of San Diego County. Here's where
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Just as a heat wave is expected to hit San Diego County starting Friday through to Oct. 8, San Diego Gas & Electric this week began notifying customers throughout the county of possible public safety power shutoffs in the next few days. Extreme heat increases energy demand on the grid and the risk of wildfires. The power shutoffs may occur from Oct. 2 at 5 a.m. through Oct. 5 at 6 p.m., potentially impacting 35,006 customers, SDG&E said. SDG&E lists the following communities that may be impacted: Alpine Boulevard Campo Descanso El Cajon Fallbrook Jamul Julian Lakeside Pala Pauma Valley Pine Valley Poway Ramona Ranchita Santa Ysabel Valley Center Warner Springs An SDG&E map shows yellow spots as areas where public safety power shutoffs may take place between Oct. 2 and Oct. 5, 2026. (SDG&E) The following are potential tribal communities that may be impacted: Barona Reservation Campo Reservation Cuyapaipe Reservation Jamul Indian Village La Jolla Reservation La Posta Reservation Los Coyotes Reservation Manzanita Reservation Mesa Grande Reservation Pala Reservation Pauma and Yuima Reservation Rincon Reservation San Pasqual Reservation Santa Ysabel Reservation Sycuan Reservation Viejas Reservation For more information on preparing for a public safety power shutoff, read SDG&E’s tips here . Power shutoffs’ impact on the Ramona community Some Ramona business owners are concerned ahead of the possible power shutoffs. Victoria Bradley is the owner of Ramona Family Naturals Market located in the Old Town Corridor in Ramona. “When the power shuts down, all the refrigeration shutdown, lights go off, and we have to get everybody out of the store,” Bradley said. Bradley is already well acquainted with the public safety power shutoffs and the inconvenience they can cause. “Most of the things in this refrigerator went into the dumpster last year,” she said. Last year, she lost about $25,000 in frozen goods during a power shutoff. Since then, any time there’s a threat of a possible public safety power shutoff, she rents a generator. She’s also rented a truck to keep her frozen goods from spoiling. “It’s a nightmare, and I can’t sell anything because it’s sitting in the back in the truck, so nobody can come and buy what they need,” she said. Bradley is one of the SDG&E customers who received a letter notifying her about a possible power shutoff impacting her market. However, when she checks the SDG&E app and types her business address, it shows it will not be impacted. “I would like to know specifically if the businesses are going to be exempt like they used to be,” she said. NBC 7 reached out to SDG&E on Thursday. The company provided the following statement: “SDG&E is closely monitoring a prolonged period of extreme heat, increased energy demand and elevated wildfire risk expected to begin Friday and continue into next week. We know these conditions can be challenging for customers, and our focus is on keeping communities safe, informed and prepared. Our teams are monitoring conditions around the clock and have positioned crews and resources across the region to respond as needed. Customers in high fire-risk areas who could be affected by a Public Safety Power Shutoff have been notified in advance, and we encourage everyone to take steps now to prepare for potential outages and extreme temperatures.”

item.title: Eurodrama in currency markets raises U.S. dollar's standing
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Data: FactSet; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios The euro fell to a 17-month low against the dollar on Monday as political and fiscal worries rattled European markets. Why it matters: Rising borrowing costs and political instability are reviving concerns about strains within the eurozone — and whether the European Central Bank may eventually have to step in. France is grappling with high deficits, rising long-term rates and political stalemate over how to address them, as our colleague Emily Peck noted . Spain's prime minister called a snap election for Nov. 29, which could strengthen Pedro Sánchez's position or open the door to a populist right government. By the numbers: The euro fell below $1.12, its lowest since May 2025 and down about 4% since Sept. 8. Between the lines: France's rising borrowing costs echo the eurozone crisis of the early 2010s, though the ECB now has more tools to contain market stress. What they're saying: In an opinion article Monday in the Financial Times, former ECB board member Lorenzo Bini Smaghi called for the central bank to suspend its quantitative tightening program in light of stress on long-term rates. Compared with the early 2010s, the ECB "is much better equipped to address tensions in financial markets that could endanger the integrity of the single currency," he wrote. "It has bond-buying tools and programmes that address spikes in yields." "However, one aspect that is more difficult to understand for observers and market participants is why, in the current stress, the ECB continues to implement its policy of quantitative tightening," he continues, or shrinking its balance sheet by not replacing government bonds as they mature. "This policy means that a larger share of the net supply of government bonds has to be absorbed by private investors, at a time when long-term rates are already under upward pressure," Bini Smaghi wrote.

item.title: The Iran war is hitting America's school buses — and kids are paying the price
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
For millions of children, the school day starts on a diesel-powered bus with a driver behind the wheel. Now, school districts are struggling to afford both. Why it matters: The Iran War is sending diesel costs higher just as districts are grappling with a yearslong bus driver shortage — a double whammy that can ripple into missed breakfasts, late classes and fewer school activities. What they're saying: "We're a non-instructional expense for a district," Peter Mannella of the National Association for Pupil Transportation tells Axios. "The inclination is always going to be let's see what we can cut out of transportation costs because we don't want to affect the school library," he says, adding that districts would rather protect spending on teachers, aides, and special education. The big picture: Districts are consolidating routes, cutting trips and squeezing more efficiency out of their fleets. A May survey of 188 school officials found 40% had adjusted routes, 27% enforced anti-idling rules, 25% cut routes, 20% limited optional trips, 14% changed fuel purchasing and 8% made students walk farther to stops. Mannella said those changes result in more parents driving students to school activities or districts moving pickup points farther from students' homes. "It starts to affect kids and families, which you know you'd rather not do," he said. Case in point: Cherry Creek Public Schools outside Denver is short about 40 drivers, transportation director Mark Ingram tells Axios. "It's an all hands on deck thing," he said. "Every morning and afternoon, we're looking at running some routes 10 to 15 minutes late … we just don't have the people to cover the routes." For some students, that can mean missing the school-provided breakfast or arriving late to first period, he said. Ingram's district has about 611 vehicles, including 320 yellow buses, plus vehicles for students with special needs and other district operations. The district budgeted $1.5 million for fuel this year, up $300,000. It now expects to spend roughly $2 million to $2.3 million. Ingram said the district hasn't cut services but is being frugal. Zoom in: The driver shortage isn't just about wages. Nick Martini, a former school bus driver who is now an executive at a Minneapolis-area school bus contractor, said drivers must simultaneously manage children and traffic while meeting extensive training, licensing and safety requirements. Split shifts can keep drivers tied up for 10 to 12 hours while paying for only a fraction of that time, and districts compete with delivery and logistics companies for the same workers with commercial-driver's licenses . Between the lines: Rural districts have even fewer escape routes. Whereas kids in urban and suburban areas can sometimes walk to school, rural children may live miles from school, requiring longer bus routes, while districts struggle to match private-sector driver pay or hire third-party operators. Special-needs transportation can be similarly expensive because curb-to-curb routes may have long gaps between stops. Flashback: The Biden administration offered federal funding to electrify school bus fleets, but some of those programs have since slowed or ended, Association of School Business Officials International's Elleka Yost tells Axios. Electric buses aren't an immediate fix everywhere. Yost pointed to narrow or winding roads, small bridges, extreme temperatures and a lack of trained technicians. The bottom line: Districts will keep adapting, Mannella said. "We are inherently problem solvers," he said. "Transportation is too important to just let us say, 'Well, we're not going to be able to do that anymore.' We'll find a way." Go deeper: School bus tech drives classroom gains
